# bv - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bv/^0.11.1/

## Expand description

The main type exported by the library, [ BitVec](https://docs.rs/struct.BitVec.html), is a packed,
growable bit-vector. Its API mirrors that of

`Vec` where reasonable.The library also defines slice operations that return
[ BitSlice](https://docs.rs/struct.BitSlice.html) or

[, akin to Rust’s array slices but for bit-vectors. A common API to bit-vectors and bit-slices is provided by the](https://docs.rs/struct.BitSliceMut.html)

`BitSliceMut`[,](https://docs.rs/trait.Bits.html)

`Bits`[, and](https://docs.rs/trait.BitsMut.html)

`BitsMut`[traits. These traits also allow treating a variety of other types as bit vectors:](https://docs.rs/trait.BitsPush.html)

`BitsPush`- all primitive unsigned integer types (*e.g.,*`u64`,`u32`),
- vectors and slices thereof (*e.g.*,`Vec<usize>`,`&[u8]`,`[u16; 4]`), and
- unpacked vectors and arrays of `bool`(*e.g.*,`[bool; 15]`).

Additionally, the [ BitsExt](https://docs.rs/trait.BitsExt.html) trait provides adapter methods including
bit-wise logic and concatenation. These adapters work for all types that implement

[.](https://docs.rs/trait.Bits.html)

`Bits`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

A first example with [ BitVec](https://docs.rs/struct.BitVec.html):

```
use bv::BitVec;
let mut bv1: BitVec = BitVec::new_fill(false, 50);
let mut bv2: BitVec = BitVec::new_fill(false, 50);
assert_eq!(bv1, bv2);
bv1.set(49, true);
assert_ne!(bv1, bv2);
assert_eq!(bv1.pop(), Some(true));
assert_eq!(bv2.pop(), Some(false));
assert_eq!(bv1, bv2);
```
Adapters, from [ BitsExt](https://docs.rs/trait.BitsExt.html) and

[:](https://docs.rs/adapter/index.html)

`adapter````
use bv::*;
use bv::adapter::BoolAdapter;
// Here, we use an `&[u16]` as a bit vector, and we adapt a
// `Vec<bool>` as well.
let array = &[0b1100u16];
let vec   = BoolAdapter::new(vec![false, true, false, true]);
// `xor` is not a `BitVec`, but a lazy adapter, thus, we can index
// it or efficiently compare it to another bit vector, without
// allocating.
let xor   = array.bit_xor(&vec);
assert_eq!( xor, bit_vec![false, true, true, false] );
```
This function performs a three-way *or*, returning a `BitVec` without
allocating an intermediate result:

```
use bv::{Bits, BitsExt, BitVec};
fn three_way_or<T, U, V>(bv1: T, bv2: U, bv3: V) -> BitVec<T::Block>
    where T: Bits,
          U: Bits<Block = T::Block>,
          V: Bits<Block = T::Block> {
    bv1.into_bit_or(bv2).into_bit_or(bv3).to_bit_vec()
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

It’s [on crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/bv), so you can add

```
[dependencies]
bv = "0.11.1"
```
to your `Cargo.toml` and

`extern crate bv;`to your crate root.

This crate supports Rust version 1.31 and newer.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [adapter](https://docs.rs/adapter/index.html)
- Lazy bit vector adapters.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- A slice of a bit-vector; akin to `&'a [bool]`but packed.
- [BitSlice](https://docs.rs/struct.BitSliceMut.html)- Mut
- A mutable slice of a bit-vector; akin to `&'a mut [bool]`but packed.
- [BitVec](https://docs.rs/struct.BitVec.html)
- A bit-vector, akin to `Vec<bool>`but packed.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [BitSliceable](https://docs.rs/trait.BitSliceable.html)
- Types that support slicing by ranges.
- [BitSliceable](https://docs.rs/trait.BitSliceableMut.html)- Mut
- Types that produce mutable slices.
- [Bits](https://docs.rs/trait.Bits.html)
- Read-only bit vector operations.
- [BitsExt](https://docs.rs/trait.BitsExt.html)
- Extension trait for adapter operations on bit slices.
- [BitsMut](https://docs.rs/trait.BitsMut.html)
- Mutable bit vector operations that don’t affect the length.
- [Bits](https://docs.rs/trait.BitsMutExt.html)- MutExt
- Extension trait for mutable operations on bit slices.
- [Bits](https://docs.rs/trait.BitsPush.html)- Push
- Bit vector operations that change the length.
- [Block](https://docs.rs/trait.BlockType.html)- Type
- Interface to primitive bit storage.

# bytes - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytes/^1.10.0/

## Expand description

Provides abstractions for working with bytes.

The `bytes` crate provides an efficient byte buffer structure
([ Bytes](https://docs.rs/struct.Bytes.html)) and traits for working with buffer
implementations (

[,](https://docs.rs/buf/trait.Buf.html)

`Buf`[).](https://docs.rs/buf/trait.BufMut.html)

`BufMut`[§](https://docs.rs#bytes)`Bytes`

`Bytes` is an efficient container for storing and operating on contiguous
slices of memory. It is intended for use primarily in networking code, but
could have applications elsewhere as well.

`Bytes` values facilitate zero-copy network programming by allowing multiple
`Bytes` objects to point to the same underlying memory. This is managed by
using a reference count to track when the memory is no longer needed and can
be freed.

A `Bytes` handle can be created directly from an existing byte store (such as `&[u8]`
or `Vec<u8>`), but usually a `BytesMut` is used first and written to. For
example:

```
use bytes::{BytesMut, BufMut};
let mut buf = BytesMut::with_capacity(1024);
buf.put(&b"hello world"[..]);
buf.put_u16(1234);
let a = buf.split();
assert_eq!(a, b"hello world\x04\xD2"[..]);
buf.put(&b"goodbye world"[..]);
let b = buf.split();
assert_eq!(b, b"goodbye world"[..]);
assert_eq!(buf.capacity(), 998);
```
In the above example, only a single buffer of 1024 is allocated. The handles
`a` and `b` will share the underlying buffer and maintain indices tracking
the view into the buffer represented by the handle.

See the [struct docs](https://docs.rs/struct.Bytes.html) for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#buf-bufmut)`Buf`, `BufMut`

These two traits provide read and write access to buffers. The underlying
storage may or may not be in contiguous memory. For example, `Bytes` is a
buffer that guarantees contiguous memory, but a [rope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rope_(data_structure)) stores the bytes in
disjoint chunks. `Buf` and `BufMut` maintain cursors tracking the current
position in the underlying byte storage. When bytes are read or written, the
cursor is advanced.

[§](https://docs.rs#relation-with-read-and-write)Relation with `Read` and `Write`

At first glance, it may seem that `Buf` and `BufMut` overlap in
functionality with [ std::io::Read](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Read.html) and

[. However, they serve different purposes. A buffer is the value that is provided as an argument to](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Write.html)

`std::io::Write``Read::read` and `Write::write`. `Read` and `Write` may then
perform a syscall, which has the potential of failing. Operations on `Buf`
and `BufMut` are infallible.## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [buf](https://docs.rs/buf/index.html)
- Utilities for working with buffers.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Bytes](https://docs.rs/struct.Bytes.html)
- A cheaply cloneable and sliceable chunk of contiguous memory.
- [Bytes](https://docs.rs/struct.BytesMut.html)- Mut
- A unique reference to a contiguous slice of memory.
- [TryGet](https://docs.rs/struct.TryGetError.html)- Error
- Error type for the `try_get_`methods of`Buf``Buf``try_get_`methods.

# log - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/log/^0.4.25/

## Expand description

A lightweight logging facade.

The `log` crate provides a single logging API that abstracts over the
actual logging implementation. Libraries can use the logging API provided
by this crate, and the consumer of those libraries can choose the logging
implementation that is most suitable for its use case.

If no logging implementation is selected, the facade falls back to a “noop” implementation that ignores all log messages. The overhead in this case is very small - just an integer load, comparison and jump.

A log request consists of a *target*, a *level*, and a *body*. A target is a
string which defaults to the module path of the location of the log request,
though that default may be overridden. Logger implementations typically use
the target to filter requests based on some user configuration.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The basic use of the log crate is through the five logging macros: [ error!](https://docs.rs/macro.error.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/macro.warn.html)

`warn!`[,](https://docs.rs/macro.info.html)

`info!`[and](https://docs.rs/macro.debug.html)

`debug!`[where](https://docs.rs/macro.trace.html)

`trace!``error!` represents the highest-priority log messages
and `trace!` the lowest. The log messages are filtered by configuring
the log level to exclude messages with a lower priority.
Each of these macros accept format strings similarly to [.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/macro.println.html)

`println!`Avoid writing expressions with side-effects in log statements. They may not be evaluated.

[§](https://docs.rs#in-libraries)In libraries

Libraries should link only to the `log` crate, and use the provided
macros to log whatever information will be useful to downstream consumers.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use log::{info, warn};
pub fn shave_the_yak(yak: &mut Yak) {
    info!(target: "yak_events", "Commencing yak shaving for {yak:?}");
    loop {
        match find_a_razor() {
            Ok(razor) => {
                info!("Razor located: {razor}");
                yak.shave(razor);
                break;
            }
            Err(err) => {
                warn!("Unable to locate a razor: {err}, retrying");
            }
        }
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#in-executables)In executables

Executables should choose a logging implementation and initialize it early in the runtime of the program. Logging implementations will typically include a function to do this. Any log messages generated before the implementation is initialized will be ignored.

The executable itself may use the `log` crate to log as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#warning)Warning

The logging system may only be initialized once.

[§](https://docs.rs#structured-logging)Structured logging

If you enable the `kv` feature you can associate structured values
with your log records. If we take the example from before, we can include
some additional context besides what’s in the formatted message:

```
use log::{info, warn};
pub fn shave_the_yak(yak: &mut Yak) {
    info!(target: "yak_events", yak:serde; "Commencing yak shaving");
    loop {
        match find_a_razor() {
            Ok(razor) => {
                info!(razor; "Razor located");
                yak.shave(razor);
                break;
            }
            Err(e) => {
                warn!(e:err; "Unable to locate a razor, retrying");
            }
        }
    }
}
```
See the [ kv](https://docs.rs/kv/index.html) module documentation for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#available-logging-implementations)Available logging implementations

In order to produce log output executables have to use a logger implementation compatible with the facade. There are many available implementations to choose from, here are some of the most popular ones:

- Simple minimal loggers:
- Complex configurable frameworks:
- Adaptors for other facilities:
- For WebAssembly binaries:
- For dynamic libraries:
- You may need to construct an FFI-safe wrapper over `log`to initialize in your libraries

- You may need to construct an FFI-safe wrapper over
- Utilities:

[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-a-logger)Implementing a Logger

Loggers implement the [ Log](https://docs.rs/trait.Log.html) trait. Here’s a very basic example that simply
logs all messages at the

[,](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Error`[or](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Warn`[levels to stdout:](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Info````
use log::{Record, Level, Metadata};
struct SimpleLogger;
impl log::Log for SimpleLogger {
    fn enabled(&self, metadata: &Metadata) -> bool {
        metadata.level() <= Level::Info
    }
    fn log(&self, record: &Record) {
        if self.enabled(record.metadata()) {
            println!("{} - {}", record.level(), record.args());
        }
    }
    fn flush(&self) {}
}
```
Loggers are installed by calling the [ set_logger](https://docs.rs/fn.set_logger.html) function. The maximum
log level also needs to be adjusted via the

[function. The logging facade uses this as an optimization to improve performance of log messages at levels that are disabled. It’s important to set it, as it defaults to](https://docs.rs/fn.set_max_level.html)

`set_max_level`[, so no log messages will ever be captured! In the case of our example logger, we’ll want to set the maximum log level to](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelFilter.html)

`Off`[, since we ignore any](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelFilter.html)

`Info`[or](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Debug`[level log messages. A logging implementation should provide a function that wraps a call to](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Trace`[and](https://docs.rs/fn.set_logger.html)

`set_logger`[, handling initialization of the logger:](https://docs.rs/fn.set_max_level.html)

`set_max_level````
use log::{SetLoggerError, LevelFilter};
static LOGGER: SimpleLogger = SimpleLogger;
pub fn init() -> Result<(), SetLoggerError> {
    log::set_logger(&LOGGER)
        .map(|()| log::set_max_level(LevelFilter::Info))
}
```
Implementations that adjust their configurations at runtime should take care to adjust the maximum log level as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#use-with-std)Use with `std`

`set_logger` requires you to provide a `&'static Log`, which can be hard to
obtain if your logger depends on some runtime configuration. The
`set_boxed_logger` function is available with the `std` Cargo feature. It is
identical to `set_logger` except that it takes a `Box<Log>` rather than a
`&'static Log`:

```
pub fn init() -> Result<(), SetLoggerError> {
    log::set_boxed_logger(Box::new(SimpleLogger))
        .map(|()| log::set_max_level(LevelFilter::Info))
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#compile-time-filters)Compile time filters

Log levels can be statically disabled at compile time by enabling one of these Cargo features:

- `max_level_off`
- `max_level_error`
- `max_level_warn`
- `max_level_info`
- `max_level_debug`
- `max_level_trace`

Log invocations at disabled levels will be skipped and will not even be present in the
resulting binary. These features control the value of the `STATIC_MAX_LEVEL` constant. The
logging macros check this value before logging a message. By default, no levels are disabled.

It is possible to override this level for release builds only with the following features:

- `release_max_level_off`
- `release_max_level_error`
- `release_max_level_warn`
- `release_max_level_info`
- `release_max_level_debug`
- `release_max_level_trace`

Libraries should avoid using the max level features because they’re global and can’t be changed once they’re set.

For example, a crate can disable trace level logs in debug builds and trace, debug, and info level logs in release builds with the following configuration:

```
[dependencies]
log = { version = "0.4", features = ["max_level_debug", "release_max_level_warn"] }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#crate-feature-flags)Crate Feature Flags

The following crate feature flags are available in addition to the filters. They are
configured in your `Cargo.toml`.

- `std`allows use of- `std`crate instead of the default- `core`. Enables using- `std::error`and- `set_boxed_logger`functionality.
- `serde`enables support for serialization and deserialization of- `Level`and- `LevelFilter`.

```
[dependencies]
log = { version = "0.4", features = ["std", "serde"] }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#version-compatibility)Version compatibility

The 0.3 and 0.4 versions of the `log` crate are almost entirely compatible. Log messages
made using `log` 0.3 will forward transparently to a logger implementation using `log` 0.4. Log
messages made using `log` 0.4 will forward to a logger implementation using `log` 0.3, but the
module path and file name information associated with the message will unfortunately be lost.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

# sha2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sha2/^0.10.8/

## Expand description

An implementation of the [SHA-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SHA-2) cryptographic hash algorithms.

There are 6 standard algorithms specified in the SHA-2 standard: [ Sha224](https://docs.rs/type.Sha224.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/type.Sha256.html)

`Sha256`[,](https://docs.rs/type.Sha512_224.html)

`Sha512_224`[,](https://docs.rs/type.Sha512_256.html)

`Sha512_256`[, and](https://docs.rs/type.Sha384.html)

`Sha384`[.](https://docs.rs/type.Sha512.html)

`Sha512`Algorithmically, there are only 2 core algorithms: SHA-256 and SHA-512. All other algorithms are just applications of these with different initial hash values, and truncated to different digest bit lengths. The first two algorithms in the list are based on SHA-256, while the last four are based on SHA-512.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

[§](https://docs.rs#one-shot-api)One-shot API

```
use hex_literal::hex;
use sha2::{Sha256, Digest};
let result = Sha256::digest(b"hello world");
assert_eq!(result[..], hex!("
    b94d27b9934d3e08a52e52d7da7dabfac484efe37a5380ee9088f7ace2efcde9
")[..]);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#incremental-api)Incremental API

```
use hex_literal::hex;
use sha2::{Sha256, Sha512, Digest};
// create a Sha256 object
let mut hasher = Sha256::new();
// write input message
hasher.update(b"hello world");
// read hash digest and consume hasher
let result = hasher.finalize();
assert_eq!(result[..], hex!("
    b94d27b9934d3e08a52e52d7da7dabfac484efe37a5380ee9088f7ace2efcde9
")[..]);
// same for Sha512
let mut hasher = Sha512::new();
hasher.update(b"hello world");
let result = hasher.finalize();
assert_eq!(result[..], hex!("
    309ecc489c12d6eb4cc40f50c902f2b4d0ed77ee511a7c7a9bcd3ca86d4cd86f
    989dd35bc5ff499670da34255b45b0cfd830e81f605dcf7dc5542e93ae9cd76f
")[..]);
```
Also see [RustCrypto/hashes](https://github.com/RustCrypto/hashes) readme.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [digest](https://docs.rs/digest/0.10.7/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/digest/index.html);

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Sha256](https://docs.rs/struct.Sha256VarCore.html)- VarCore
- Core block-level SHA-256 hasher with variable output size.
- [Sha512](https://docs.rs/struct.Sha512VarCore.html)- VarCore
- Core block-level SHA-512 hasher with variable output size.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Digest](https://docs.rs/trait.Digest.html)
- Convenience wrapper trait covering functionality of cryptographic hash functions with fixed output size.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [compress256](https://docs.rs/fn.compress256.html)- `compress`
- Raw SHA-256 compression function.
- [compress512](https://docs.rs/fn.compress512.html)- `compress`
- Raw SHA-512 compression function.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Sha224](https://docs.rs/type.Sha224.html)
- SHA-224 hasher.
- [Sha256](https://docs.rs/type.Sha256.html)
- SHA-256 hasher.
- [Sha384](https://docs.rs/type.Sha384.html)
- SHA-384 hasher.
- [Sha512](https://docs.rs/type.Sha512.html)
- SHA-512 hasher.
- [Sha512_](https://docs.rs/type.Sha512_224.html)- 224
- SHA-512/224 hasher.
- [Sha512_](https://docs.rs/type.Sha512_256.html)- 256
- SHA-512/256 hasher.

# thiserror - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/thiserror/^2.0.18/

## Expand description

This library provides a convenient derive macro for the standard library’s
[ std::error::Error](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/error/trait.Error.html) trait.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use thiserror::Error;
#[derive(Error, Debug)]
pub enum DataStoreError {
    #[error("data store disconnected")]
    Disconnect(#[from] io::Error),
    #[error("the data for key `{0}` is not available")]
    Redaction(String),
    #[error("invalid header (expected {expected:?}, found {found:?})")]
    InvalidHeader {
        expected: String,
        found: String,
    },
    #[error("unknown data store error")]
    Unknown,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#details)Details

-
Thiserror deliberately does not appear in your public API. You get the same thing as if you had written an implementation of `std::error::Error`
-
Errors may be enums, structs with named fields, tuple structs, or unit structs.
-
A `Display``#[error("...")]`messages on the struct or each variant of your enum, as shown above in the example.The messages support a shorthand for interpolating fields from the error. - `#[error("{var}")]`⟶- `write!("{}", self.var)`
- `#[error("{0}")]`⟶- `write!("{}", self.0)`
- `#[error("{var:?}")]`⟶- `write!("{:?}", self.var)`
- `#[error("{0:?}")]`⟶- `write!("{:?}", self.0)`
 These shorthands can be used together with any additional format args, which may be arbitrary expressions. For example: `#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum Error { #[error("invalid rdo_lookahead_frames {0} (expected < {max})", max = i32::MAX)] InvalidLookahead(u32), }`If one of the additional expression arguments needs to refer to a field of the struct or enum, then refer to named fields as `.var`and tuple fields as`.0`.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum Error { #[error("first letter must be lowercase but was {:?}", first_char(.0))] WrongCase(String), #[error("invalid index {idx}, expected at least {} and at most {}", .limits.lo, .limits.hi)] OutOfBounds { idx: usize, limits: Limits }, }`
-
A `From``#[from]`attribute.The variant using `#[from]`must not contain any other fields beyond the source error (and possibly a backtrace — see below). Usually`#[from]`fields are unnamed, but`#[from]`is allowed on a named field too.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { Io(#[from] io::Error), Glob(#[from] globset::Error), }`
-
The Error trait’s `source()``#[source]`attribute or is named`source`, if any. This is for identifying the underlying lower level error that caused your error.The `#[from]`attribute always implies that the same field is`#[source]`, so you don’t ever need to specify both attributes.Any error type that implements `std::error::Error`or dereferences to`dyn std::error::Error`will work as a source.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub struct MyError { msg: String, #[source] // optional if field name is `source` source: anyhow::Error, }`
-
The Error trait’s `provide()``Backtrace`, if any, as a`std::backtrace::Backtrace``Backtrace`in errors requires a nightly compiler with Rust version 1.73 or newer.`use std::backtrace::Backtrace; #[derive(Error, Debug)] pub struct MyError { msg: String, backtrace: Backtrace, // automatically detected }`
-
If a field is both a source (named `source`, or has`#[source]`or`#[from]`attribute)*and*is marked`#[backtrace]`, then the Error trait’s`provide()``provide`so that both layers of the error share the same backtrace. The`#[backtrace]`attribute requires a nightly compiler with Rust version 1.73 or newer.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { Io { #[backtrace] source: io::Error, }, }`
-
For variants that use `#[from]`and also contain a`Backtrace`field, a backtrace is captured from within the`From`impl.`#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { Io { #[from] source: io::Error, backtrace: Backtrace, }, }`
-
Errors may use `error(transparent)`to forward the source and`Display``#[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum MyError { ... #[error(transparent)] Other(#[from] anyhow::Error), // source and Display delegate to anyhow::Error }`Another use case is hiding implementation details of an error representation behind an opaque error type, so that the representation is able to evolve without breaking the crate’s public API. `// PublicError is public, but opaque and easy to keep compatible. #[derive(Error, Debug)] #[error(transparent)] pub struct PublicError(#[from] ErrorRepr); impl PublicError { // Accessors for anything we do want to expose publicly. } // Private and free to change across minor version of the crate. #[derive(Error, Debug)] enum ErrorRepr { ... }`
-
See also the `anyhow`

# bincode - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bincode/^1.3.3/

## Expand description

Bincode is a crate for encoding and decoding using a tiny binary serialization strategy. Using it, you can easily go from having an object in memory, quickly serialize it to bytes, and then deserialize it back just as fast!

[§](https://docs.rs#using-basic-functions)Using Basic Functions

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fn main() {
    // The object that we will serialize.
    let target: Option<String>  = Some("hello world".to_string());
    let encoded: Vec<u8> = bincode::serialize(&target).unwrap();
    let decoded: Option<String> = bincode::deserialize(&encoded[..]).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(target, decoded);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#128bit-numbers)128bit numbers

Support for `i128` and `u128` is automatically enabled on Rust toolchains
greater than or equal to `1.26.0` and disabled for targets which do not support it

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use config::`- [DefaultOptions](https://docs.rs/config/struct.DefaultOptions.html);
- `pub use config::`- [Options](https://docs.rs/config/trait.Options.html);
- `pub use de::read::`- [BincodeRead](https://docs.rs/de/read/trait.BincodeRead.html);
- `pub use de::`- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/de/struct.Deserializer.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Deserialize bincode data to a Rust data structure.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [config](https://docs.rs/fn.config.html)- Deprecated

- [deserialize](https://docs.rs/fn.deserialize.html)
- Deserializes a slice of bytes into an instance of `T`using the default configuration.
- [deserialize_](https://docs.rs/fn.deserialize_from.html)- from

- [deserialize_](https://docs.rs/fn.deserialize_from_custom.html)- from_ - custom

# memmap2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/memmap2/^0.5.10/

## Expand description

A cross-platform Rust API for memory mapped buffers.

The core functionality is provided by either [ Mmap](https://docs.rs/struct.Mmap.html) or

[, which correspond to mapping a](https://docs.rs/struct.MmapMut.html)

`MmapMut`[to a](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/fs/struct.File.html)

`File`[or](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.slice.html)

`&[u8]`[respectively. Both function by dereferencing to a slice, allowing the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.slice.html)

`&mut [u8]`[/](https://docs.rs/struct.Mmap.html)

`Mmap`[to be used in the same way you would the equivelant slice types.](https://docs.rs/struct.MmapMut.html)

`MmapMut`For simple cases [ Mmap](https://docs.rs/struct.Mmap.html) can be used directly:

```
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::Read;
use memmap2::Mmap;
let mut file = File::open("LICENSE-APACHE")?;
let mut contents = Vec::new();
file.read_to_end(&mut contents)?;
let mmap = unsafe { Mmap::map(&file)?  };
assert_eq!(&contents[..], &mmap[..]);
```
However for cases which require configuration of the mapping, then
you can use [ MmapOptions](https://docs.rs/struct.MmapOptions.html) in order to further configure a mapping
before you create it.

- A handle to an immutable memory mapped buffer.
- A handle to a mutable memory mapped buffer.
- A memory map builder, providing advanced options and flags for specifying memory map behavior.
- A handle to a raw memory mapped buffer.

# rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.9.2/

## Expand description

Utilities for random number generation

Rand provides utilities to generate random numbers, to convert them to useful types and distributions, and some randomness-related algorithms.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
// The prelude import enables methods we use below, specifically
// Rng::random, Rng::sample, SliceRandom::shuffle and IndexedRandom::choose.
use rand::prelude::*;
// Get an RNG:
let mut rng = rand::rng();
// Try printing a random unicode code point (probably a bad idea)!
println!("char: '{}'", rng.random::<char>());
// Try printing a random alphanumeric value instead!
println!("alpha: '{}'", rng.sample(rand::distr::Alphanumeric) as char);
// Generate and shuffle a sequence:
let mut nums: Vec<i32> = (1..100).collect();
nums.shuffle(&mut rng);
// And take a random pick (yes, we didn't need to shuffle first!):
let _ = nums.choose(&mut rng);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-book)The Book

For the user guide and further documentation, please read
[The Rust Rand Book](https://rust-random.github.io/book).

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

# rand_chacha - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_chacha/^0.9.0/

## Expand description

The ChaCha random number generators.

These are native Rust implementations of RNGs derived from the
[ChaCha stream ciphers](https://cr.yp.to/chacha.html) by D J Bernstein.

[§](https://docs.rs#generators)Generators

This crate provides 8-, 12- and 20-round variants of generators via a “core”
implementation (of [ BlockRngCore](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.9.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/block/trait.BlockRngCore.html)), each with an associated “RNG” type
(implementing

[).](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.9.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/trait.RngCore.html)

`RngCore`These generators are all deterministic and portable (see [Reproducibility](https://rust-random.github.io/book/crate-reprod.html)
in the book), with testing against reference vectors.

[§](https://docs.rs#cryptographic-secure-usage)Cryptographic (secure) usage

Where secure unpredictable generators are required, it is suggested to use
[ ChaCha12Rng](https://docs.rs/struct.ChaCha12Rng.html) or

[and to seed via](https://docs.rs/struct.ChaCha20Rng.html)

`ChaCha20Rng`[.](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.9.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/trait.SeedableRng.html#method.from_os_rng)

`SeedableRng::from_os_rng`See also the [Security](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-rngs.html#security) chapter in the rand book. The crate is provided
“as is”, without any form of guarantee, and without a security audit.

[§](https://docs.rs#seeding-construction)Seeding (construction)

Generators implement the [ SeedableRng](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.9.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/trait.SeedableRng.html) trait. Any method may be used,
but note that

`seed_from_u64` is not suitable for usage where security is
important. Some suggestions:- With a fresh seed, **direct from the OS**(implies a syscall):`let rng = ChaCha12Rng::from_os_rng();`
- **From a master generator.**This could be- `rand::rng`- `ChaCha20Rng`

See also [Seeding RNGs](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-seeding.html) in the book.

[§](https://docs.rs#generation)Generation

Generators implement [ RngCore](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.9.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/trait.RngCore.html), whose methods may be used directly to
generate unbounded integer or byte values.

```
use rand_core::{SeedableRng, RngCore};
use rand_chacha::ChaCha12Rng;
let mut rng = ChaCha12Rng::from_seed(Default::default());
let x = rng.next_u64();
assert_eq!(x, 0x53f955076a9af49b);
```
It is often more convenient to use the [ rand::Rng](https://docs.rs/rand/latest/rand/fn.rng.html) trait, which provides
further functionality. See also the

[Random Values](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-values.html)chapter in the book.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [rand_core](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.9.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/index.html);

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [ChaCha8](https://docs.rs/struct.ChaCha8Core.html)- Core
- ChaCha with 8 rounds
- [ChaCha8](https://docs.rs/struct.ChaCha8Rng.html)- Rng
- A cryptographically secure random number generator that uses the ChaCha algorithm.

# bitflags - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bitflags/^2.8.0/

## Expand description

Generate types for C-style flags with ergonomic APIs.

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting started

Add `bitflags` to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies.bitflags]
version = "2.13.0"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#crate-features)Crate features

The `bitflags` library defines a few Cargo features that you can opt-in to:

- `std`: Implement the- `Error`trait on error types used by- `bitflags`.
- `serde`: Support deriving- `serde`traits on generated flags types.
- `arbitrary`: Support deriving- `arbitrary`traits on generated flags types.
- `bytemuck`: Support deriving- `bytemuck`traits on generated flags types.

[§](https://docs.rs#generating-flags-types)Generating flags types

Use the [ bitflags](https://docs.rs/macro.bitflags.html) macro to generate flags types:

```
use bitflags::bitflags;
bitflags! {
    pub struct Flags: u32 {
        const A = 0b00000001;
        const B = 0b00000010;
        const C = 0b00000100;
    }
}
```
See the docs for the `bitflags` macro for the full syntax.

Also see the [ example_generated](https://docs.rs/example_generated/index.html) module for an example of what the

`bitflags` macro generates for a flags type.[§](https://docs.rs#externally-defined-flags)Externally defined flags

If you’re generating flags types for an external source, such as a C API, you can define
an extra unnamed flag as a mask of all bits the external source may ever set. Usually this would be all bits (`!0`):

```
bitflags! {
    pub struct Flags: u32 {
        const A = 0b00000001;
        const B = 0b00000010;
        const C = 0b00000100;
        // The source may set any bits
        const _ = !0;
    }
}
```
Why should you do this? Generated methods like `all` and truncating operators like `!` only consider
bits in defined flags. Adding an unnamed flag makes those methods consider additional bits,
without generating additional constants for them. It helps compatibility when the external source
may start setting additional bits at any time. The [known and unknown bits](https://docs.rs#known-and-unknown-bits)
section has more details on this behavior.

[§](https://docs.rs#custom-derives)Custom derives

You can derive some traits on generated flags types if you enable Cargo features. The following libraries are currently supported:

- `serde`: Support- `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]`, using text for human-readable formats, and a raw number for binary formats.
- `arbitrary`: Support- `#[derive(Arbitrary)]`, only generating flags values with known bits.
- `bytemuck`: Support- `#[derive(Pod, Zeroable)]`, for casting between flags values and their underlying bits values.

You can also define your own flags type outside of the [ bitflags](https://docs.rs/macro.bitflags.html) macro and then use it to generate methods.
This can be useful if you need a custom

`#[derive]` attribute for a library that `bitflags` doesn’t
natively support:```
#[derive(SomeTrait)]
pub struct Flags(u32);
bitflags! {
    impl Flags: u32 {
        const A = 0b00000001;
        const B = 0b00000010;
        const C = 0b00000100;
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#adding-custom-methods)Adding custom methods

The [ bitflags](https://docs.rs/macro.bitflags.html) macro supports attributes on generated flags types within the macro itself, while

`impl` blocks can be added outside of it:```
bitflags! {
    // Attributes can be applied to flags types
    #[repr(transparent)]
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
    pub struct Flags: u32 {
        const A = 0b00000001;
        const B = 0b00000010;
        const C = 0b00000100;
    }
}
// Impl blocks can be added to flags types
impl Flags {
    pub fn as_u64(&self) -> u64 {
        self.bits() as u64
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#renaming-flags)Renaming flags

The [ bitflags](https://docs.rs/macro.bitflags.html) macro recognizes a special

`#[bitflags(flag_name = "<value>")]` attribute on flags values to rename them:```
bitflags! {
    pub struct Flags: u32 {
        // Add the attribute to a flag to change its name
        #[bitflags(flag_name = "a")]
        const A = 0b00000001;
        #[bitflags(flag_name = "b")]
        const B = 0b00000010;
        #[bitflags(flag_name = "c")]
        const C = 0b00000100;
    }
}
```
When applied to a flag value, instead of using its identifier, like `A` as the name, it’ll use the given string. This
doesn’t affect the identifier of the constant itself, just the name recognized when parsing and formatting.

[§](https://docs.rs#working-with-flags-values)Working with flags values

Use generated constants and standard bitwise operators to interact with flags values:

```
// union
let ab = Flags::A | Flags::B;
// intersection
let a = ab & Flags::A;
// difference
let b = ab - Flags::A;
// complement
let c = !ab;
```
See the docs for the [ Flags](https://docs.rs/trait.Flags.html) trait for more details on operators and how they behave.

[§](https://docs.rs#formatting-and-parsing)Formatting and parsing

`bitflags` defines a text format that can be used to convert any flags value to and from strings.

See the [ parser](https://docs.rs/parser/index.html) module for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#specification)Specification

The terminology and behavior of generated flags types is
[specified in the source repository](https://github.com/bitflags/bitflags/blob/main/spec.md).
Details are repeated in these docs where appropriate, but is exhaustively listed in the spec. Some
things are worth calling out explicitly here.

[§](https://docs.rs#flags-types-flags-values-flags)Flags types, flags values, flags

The spec and these docs use consistent terminology to refer to things in the bitflags domain:

- **Bits type**: A type that defines a fixed number of bits at specific locations.
- **Flag**: A set of bits in a bits type that may have a unique name.
- **Flags type**: A set of defined flags over a specific bits type.
- **Flags value**: An instance of a flags type using its specific bits value for storage.

```
bitflags! {
    struct FlagsType: u8 {
//                    -- Bits type
//         --------- Flags type
        const A = 1;
//            ----- Flag
    }
}
let flag = FlagsType::A;
//  ---- Flags value
```
[§](https://docs.rs#known-and-unknown-bits)Known and unknown bits

Any bits in a flag you define are called *known bits*. Any other bits are *unknown bits*.
In the following flags type:

```
bitflags! {
    struct Flags: u8 {
        const A = 1;
        const B = 1 << 1;
        const C = 1 << 2;
    }
}
```
The known bits are `0b0000_0111` and the unknown bits are `0b1111_1000`.

`bitflags` doesn’t guarantee that a flags value will only ever have known bits set, but some operators
will unset any unknown bits they encounter. In a future version of `bitflags`, all operators will
unset unknown bits.

If you’re using `bitflags` for flags types defined externally, such as from C, you probably want all
bits to be considered known, in case that external source changes. You can do this using an unnamed
flag, as described in [externally defined flags](https://docs.rs#externally-defined-flags).

[§](https://docs.rs#zero-bit-flags)Zero-bit flags

Flags with no bits set should be avoided because they interact strangely with [ Flags::contains](https://docs.rs/trait.Flags.html#method.contains)
and

[. A zero-bit flag is always contained, but is never intersected. The names of zero-bit flags can be parsed, but are never formatted.](https://docs.rs/trait.Flags.html#method.intersects)

`Flags::intersects`[§](https://docs.rs#multi-bit-flags)Multi-bit flags

Flags that set multiple bits should be avoided unless each bit is also in a single-bit flag. Take the following flags type as an example:

```
bitflags! {
    struct Flags: u8 {
        const A = 1;
        const B = 1 | 1 << 1;
    }
}
```
The result of `Flags::A ^ Flags::B` is `0b0000_0010`, which doesn’t correspond to either
`Flags::A` or `Flags::B` even though it’s still a known bit.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [example_](https://docs.rs/example_generated/index.html)- generated
- This module shows an example of code generated by the macro. **IT MUST NOT BE USED OUTSIDE THIS CRATE**.
- [iter](https://docs.rs/iter/index.html)
- Yield the bits of a source flags value in a set of contained flags values.
- [parser](https://docs.rs/parser/index.html)
- Parsing flags from text.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [bitflags](https://docs.rs/macro.bitflags.html)
- Generate a flags type.
- [bitflags_](https://docs.rs/macro.bitflags_match.html)- match
- A macro that matches flags values, similar to Rust’s `match`statement.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Flag](https://docs.rs/struct.Flag.html)
- A defined flags value that may be named or unnamed.

# bincode - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bincode/1.3.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/bincode/index.html

## Expand description

Bincode is a crate for encoding and decoding using a tiny binary serialization strategy. Using it, you can easily go from having an object in memory, quickly serialize it to bytes, and then deserialize it back just as fast!

[§](https://docs.rs#using-basic-functions)Using Basic Functions

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fn main() {
    // The object that we will serialize.
    let target: Option<String>  = Some("hello world".to_string());
    let encoded: Vec<u8> = bincode::serialize(&target).unwrap();
    let decoded: Option<String> = bincode::deserialize(&encoded[..]).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(target, decoded);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#128bit-numbers)128bit numbers

Support for `i128` and `u128` is automatically enabled on Rust toolchains
greater than or equal to `1.26.0` and disabled for targets which do not support it

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use config::`- [Config](https://docs.rs/config/struct.Config.html);- Deprecated
- `pub use config::`- [DefaultOptions](https://docs.rs/config/struct.DefaultOptions.html);
- `pub use config::`- [Options](https://docs.rs/config/trait.Options.html);
- `pub use de::read::`- [BincodeRead](https://docs.rs/de/read/trait.BincodeRead.html);
- `pub use de::`- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/de/struct.Deserializer.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [config](https://docs.rs/config/index.html)
- `bincode`uses a Builder-pattern to configure the Serializers and Deserializers in this crate. This means that if you need to customize the behavior of- `bincode`, you should create an instance of the- `DefaultOptions`struct:
- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Deserialize bincode data to a Rust data structure.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/struct.Serializer.html)
- An Serializer that encodes values directly into a Writer.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.ErrorKind.html)- Kind
- The kind of error that can be produced during a serialization or deserialization.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [config](https://docs.rs/fn.config.html)- Deprecated
- Get a default configuration object.
- [deserialize](https://docs.rs/fn.deserialize.html)
- Deserializes a slice of bytes into an instance of `T`using the default configuration.
- [deserialize_](https://docs.rs/fn.deserialize_from.html)- from
- Deserializes an object directly from a `Read`er using the default configuration.
- [deserialize_](https://docs.rs/fn.deserialize_from_custom.html)- from_ - custom
- Deserializes an object from a custom `BincodeRead`er using the default configuration. It is highly recommended to use`deserialize_from`unless you need to implement`BincodeRead`for performance reasons.
- [options](https://docs.rs/fn.options.html)
- Get a default configuration object.
- [serialize](https://docs.rs/fn.serialize.html)
- Serializes a serializable object into a `Vec`of bytes using the default configuration.
- [serialize_](https://docs.rs/fn.serialize_into.html)- into
- Serializes an object directly into a `Writer`using the default configuration.
- [serialized_](https://docs.rs/fn.serialized_size.html)- size
- Returns the size that an object would be if serialized using Bincode with the default configuration.

# rand_chacha - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_chacha/0.9.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_chacha/index.html

## Expand description

The ChaCha random number generators.

These are native Rust implementations of RNGs derived from the
[ChaCha stream ciphers](https://cr.yp.to/chacha.html) by D J Bernstein.

[§](https://docs.rs#generators)Generators

This crate provides 8-, 12- and 20-round variants of generators via a “core”
implementation (of [ BlockRngCore](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.9.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/block/trait.BlockRngCore.html)), each with an associated “RNG” type
(implementing

[).](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.9.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/trait.RngCore.html)

`RngCore`These generators are all deterministic and portable (see [Reproducibility](https://rust-random.github.io/book/crate-reprod.html)
in the book), with testing against reference vectors.

[§](https://docs.rs#cryptographic-secure-usage)Cryptographic (secure) usage

Where secure unpredictable generators are required, it is suggested to use
[ ChaCha12Rng](https://docs.rs/struct.ChaCha12Rng.html) or

[and to seed via](https://docs.rs/struct.ChaCha20Rng.html)

`ChaCha20Rng`[.](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.9.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/trait.SeedableRng.html#method.from_os_rng)

`SeedableRng::from_os_rng`See also the [Security](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-rngs.html#security) chapter in the rand book. The crate is provided
“as is”, without any form of guarantee, and without a security audit.

[§](https://docs.rs#seeding-construction)Seeding (construction)

Generators implement the [ SeedableRng](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.9.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/trait.SeedableRng.html) trait. Any method may be used,
but note that

`seed_from_u64` is not suitable for usage where security is
important. Some suggestions:- With a fresh seed, **direct from the OS**(implies a syscall):`let rng = ChaCha12Rng::from_os_rng();`
- **From a master generator.**This could be- `rand::rng`- `ChaCha20Rng`

See also [Seeding RNGs](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-seeding.html) in the book.

[§](https://docs.rs#generation)Generation

Generators implement [ RngCore](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.9.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/trait.RngCore.html), whose methods may be used directly to
generate unbounded integer or byte values.

```
use rand_core::{SeedableRng, RngCore};
use rand_chacha::ChaCha12Rng;
let mut rng = ChaCha12Rng::from_seed(Default::default());
let x = rng.next_u64();
assert_eq!(x, 0x53f955076a9af49b);
```
It is often more convenient to use the [ rand::Rng](https://docs.rs/rand/latest/rand/fn.rng.html) trait, which provides
further functionality. See also the

[Random Values](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-values.html)chapter in the book.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [rand_core](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.9.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/index.html);

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [ChaCha8](https://docs.rs/struct.ChaCha8Core.html)- Core
- ChaCha with 8 rounds
- [ChaCha8](https://docs.rs/struct.ChaCha8Rng.html)- Rng
- A cryptographically secure random number generator that uses the ChaCha algorithm.
- [ChaCha12](https://docs.rs/struct.ChaCha12Core.html)- Core
- ChaCha with 12 rounds
- [ChaCha12](https://docs.rs/struct.ChaCha12Rng.html)- Rng
- A cryptographically secure random number generator that uses the ChaCha algorithm.
- [ChaCha20](https://docs.rs/struct.ChaCha20Core.html)- Core
- ChaCha with 20 rounds
- [ChaCha20](https://docs.rs/struct.ChaCha20Rng.html)- Rng
- A cryptographically secure random number generator that uses the ChaCha algorithm.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [ChaCha](https://docs.rs/type.ChaChaCore.html)- Core
- ChaCha with 20 rounds, low-level interface
- [ChaCha](https://docs.rs/type.ChaChaRng.html)- Rng
- ChaCha with 20 rounds

# proc_macro2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/^1.0.106/

## Expand description

A wrapper around the procedural macro API of the compiler’s [ proc_macro](https://doc.rust-lang.org/proc_macro/index.html)
crate. This library serves two purposes:

-
**Bring proc-macro-like functionality to other contexts like build.rs and main.rs.**Types from`proc_macro`are entirely specific to procedural macros and cannot ever exist in code outside of a procedural macro. Meanwhile`proc_macro2`types may exist anywhere including non-macro code. By developing foundational libraries like[syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn)and[quote](https://github.com/dtolnay/quote)against`proc_macro2`rather than`proc_macro`, the procedural macro ecosystem becomes easily applicable to many other use cases and we avoid reimplementing non-macro equivalents of those libraries.
-
**Make procedural macros unit testable.**As a consequence of being specific to procedural macros, nothing that uses`proc_macro`can be executed from a unit test. In order for helper libraries or components of a macro to be testable in isolation, they must be implemented using`proc_macro2`.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The skeleton of a typical procedural macro typically looks like this:

```
extern crate proc_macro;
#[proc_macro_derive(MyDerive)]
pub fn my_derive(input: proc_macro::TokenStream) -> proc_macro::TokenStream {
    let input = proc_macro2::TokenStream::from(input);
    let output: proc_macro2::TokenStream = {
        /* transform input */
    };
    proc_macro::TokenStream::from(output)
}
```
If parsing with [Syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn), you’ll use [ parse_macro_input!](https://docs.rs/syn/2.0/syn/macro.parse_macro_input.html) instead to
propagate parse errors correctly back to the compiler when parsing fails.

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-features)Unstable features

The default feature set of proc-macro2 tracks the most recent stable
compiler API. Functionality in `proc_macro` that is not yet stable is not
exposed by proc-macro2 by default.

To opt into the additional APIs available in the most recent nightly
compiler, the `procmacro2_semver_exempt` config flag must be passed to
rustc. We will polyfill those nightly-only APIs back to Rust 1.68.0. As
these are unstable APIs that track the nightly compiler, minor versions of
proc-macro2 may make breaking changes to them at any time.

`RUSTFLAGS='--cfg procmacro2_semver_exempt' cargo build`Note that this must not only be done for your crate, but for any crate that depends on your crate. This infectious nature is intentional, as it serves as a reminder that you are outside of the normal semver guarantees.

Semver exempt methods are marked as such in the proc-macro2 documentation.

[§](https://docs.rs#thread-safety)Thread-Safety

Most types in this crate are `!Sync` because the underlying compiler
types make use of thread-local memory, meaning they cannot be accessed from
a different thread.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [extra](https://docs.rs/extra/index.html)
- Items which do not have a correspondence to any API in the proc_macro crate, but are necessary to include in proc-macro2.
- [token_](https://docs.rs/token_stream/index.html)- stream
- Public implementation details for the `TokenStream`type, such as iterators.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Group](https://docs.rs/struct.Group.html)
- A delimited token stream.
- [Ident](https://docs.rs/struct.Ident.html)
- A word of Rust code, which may be a keyword or legal variable name.
- [LexError](https://docs.rs/struct.LexError.html)
- Error returned from `TokenStream::from_str`.
- [Line](https://docs.rs/struct.LineColumn.html)- Column - `span-locations`
- A line-column pair representing the start or end of a `Span`.
- [Literal](https://docs.rs/struct.Literal.html)
- A literal string (`"hello"`), byte string (`b"hello"`), character (`'a'`), byte character (`b'a'`), an integer or floating point number with or without a suffix (`1`,`1u8`,`2.3`,`2.3f32`).
- [Punct](https://docs.rs/struct.Punct.html)
- A `Punct`is a single punctuation character like`+`,`-`or`#`.
- [Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)
- A region of source code, along with macro expansion information.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/struct.TokenStream.html)- Stream
- An abstract stream of tokens, or more concretely a sequence of token trees.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Conversion](https://docs.rs/enum.ConversionErrorKind.html)- Error - Kind - `procmacro2_semver_exempt`
- Error when retrieving a string literal’s unescaped value.
- [Delimiter](https://docs.rs/enum.Delimiter.html)
- Describes how a sequence of token trees is delimited.
- [Escape](https://docs.rs/enum.EscapeError.html)- Error - `procmacro2_semver_exempt`
- Errors and warnings that can occur during string, char, and byte unescaping.
- [Spacing](https://docs.rs/enum.Spacing.html)
- Whether a `Punct`is followed immediately by another`Punct`or followed by another token or whitespace.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/enum.TokenTree.html)- Tree
- A single token or a delimited sequence of token trees (e.g. `[1, (), ..]`).

# quote - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quote/^1.0.45/

## Expand description

This crate provides the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html) macro for turning Rust syntax tree data
structures into tokens of source code.

Procedural macros in Rust receive a stream of tokens as input, execute arbitrary Rust code to determine how to manipulate those tokens, and produce a stream of tokens to hand back to the compiler to compile into the caller’s crate. Quasi-quoting is a solution to one piece of that — producing tokens to return to the compiler.

The idea of quasi-quoting is that we write *code* that we treat as *data*.
Within the `quote!` macro, we can write what looks like code to our text
editor or IDE. We get all the benefits of the editor’s brace matching,
syntax highlighting, indentation, and maybe autocompletion. But rather than
compiling that as code into the current crate, we can treat it as data, pass
it around, mutate it, and eventually hand it back to the compiler as tokens
to compile into the macro caller’s crate.

This crate is motivated by the procedural macro use case, but is a general-purpose Rust quasi-quoting library and is not specific to procedural macros.

```
[dependencies]
quote = "1.0"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

The following quasi-quoted block of code is something you might find in [a](https://serde.rs/)
procedural macro having to do with data structure serialization. The `#var`
syntax performs interpolation of runtime variables into the quoted tokens.
Check out the documentation of the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html) macro for more detail about
the syntax. See also the

[macro which is important for implementing hygienic procedural macros.](https://docs.rs/macro.quote_spanned.html)

`quote_spanned!````
let tokens = quote! {
    struct SerializeWith #generics #where_clause {
        value: &'a #field_ty,
        phantom: core::marker::PhantomData<#item_ty>,
    }
    impl #generics serde::Serialize for SerializeWith #generics #where_clause {
        fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
        where
            S: serde::Serializer,
        {
            #path(self.value, serializer)
        }
    }
    SerializeWith {
        value: #value,
        phantom: core::marker::PhantomData::<#item_ty>,
    }
};
```
[§](https://docs.rs#non-macro-code-generators)Non-macro code generators

When using `quote` in a build.rs or main.rs and writing the output out to a
file, consider having the code generator pass the tokens through
[prettyplease](https://github.com/dtolnay/prettyplease) before writing. This way if an error occurs in the generated
code it is convenient for a human to read and debug.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [format_](https://docs.rs/macro.format_ident.html)- ident
- Formatting macro for constructing `Ident`s.
- [quote](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html)
- The whole point.
- [quote_](https://docs.rs/macro.quote_spanned.html)- spanned
- Same as `quote!`, but applies a given span to all tokens originating within the macro invocation.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Ident](https://docs.rs/trait.IdentFragment.html)- Fragment
- Specialized formatting trait used by `format_ident!`.
- [ToTokens](https://docs.rs/trait.ToTokens.html)
- Types that can be interpolated inside a `quote!`invocation.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/trait.TokenStreamExt.html)- Stream - Ext
- TokenStream extension trait with methods for appending tokens.

---

# syn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/syn/^2.0.117/

## Expand description

Syn is a parsing library for parsing a stream of Rust tokens into a syntax tree of Rust source code.

Currently this library is geared toward use in Rust procedural macros, but contains some APIs that may be useful more generally.

-
**Data structures**— Syn provides a complete syntax tree that can represent any valid Rust source code. The syntax tree is rooted at`syn::File``syn::Item``syn::Expr``syn::Type`
-
**Derives**— Of particular interest to derive macros is`syn::DeriveInput`
-
**Parsing**— Parsing in Syn is built around[parser functions](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)with the signature`fn(ParseStream) -> Result<T>`. Every syntax tree node defined by Syn is individually parsable and may be used as a building block for custom syntaxes, or you may dream up your own brand new syntax without involving any of our syntax tree types.
-
**Location information**— Every token parsed by Syn is associated with a`Span`that tracks line and column information back to the source of that token. These spans allow a procedural macro to display detailed error messages pointing to all the right places in the user’s code. There is an example of this below.
-
**Feature flags**— Functionality is aggressively feature gated so your procedural macros enable only what they need, and do not pay in compile time for all the rest.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-of-a-derive-macro)Example of a derive macro

The canonical derive macro using Syn looks like this. We write an ordinary
Rust function tagged with a `proc_macro_derive` attribute and the name of
the trait we are deriving. Any time that derive appears in the user’s code,
the Rust compiler passes their data structure as tokens into our macro. We
get to execute arbitrary Rust code to figure out what to do with those
tokens, then hand some tokens back to the compiler to compile into the
user’s crate.

```
[dependencies]
syn = "2.0"
quote = "1.0"
[lib]
proc-macro = true
```
```
use proc_macro::TokenStream;
use quote::quote;
use syn::{parse_macro_input, DeriveInput};
#[proc_macro_derive(MyMacro)]
pub fn my_macro(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    // Parse the input tokens into a syntax tree
    let input = parse_macro_input!(input as DeriveInput);
    // Build the output, possibly using quasi-quotation
    let expanded = quote! {
        // ...
    };
    // Hand the output tokens back to the compiler
    TokenStream::from(expanded)
}
```
The [ heapsize](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/heapsize) example directory shows a complete working implementation
of a derive macro. The example derives a

`HeapSize` trait which computes an
estimate of the amount of heap memory owned by a value.```
pub trait HeapSize {
    /// Total number of bytes of heap memory owned by `self`.
    fn heap_size_of_children(&self) -> usize;
}
```
The derive macro allows users to write `#[derive(HeapSize)]` on data
structures in their program.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Demo<'a, T: ?Sized> {
    a: Box<T>,
    b: u8,
    c: &'a str,
    d: String,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#spans-and-error-reporting)Spans and error reporting

The token-based procedural macro API provides great control over where the
compiler’s error messages are displayed in user code. Consider the error the
user sees if one of their field types does not implement `HeapSize`.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Broken {
    ok: String,
    bad: std::thread::Thread,
}
```
By tracking span information all the way through the expansion of a
procedural macro as shown in the `heapsize` example, token-based macros in
Syn are able to trigger errors that directly pinpoint the source of the
problem.

```
error[E0277]: the trait bound `std::thread::Thread: HeapSize` is not satisfied
 --> src/main.rs:7:5
  |
7 |     bad: std::thread::Thread,
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the trait `HeapSize` is not implemented for `Thread`
```
[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-a-custom-syntax)Parsing a custom syntax

The [ lazy-static](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/lazy-static) example directory shows the implementation of a

`functionlike!(...)` procedural macro in which the input tokens are parsed
using Syn’s parsing API.The example reimplements the popular `lazy_static` crate from crates.io as a
procedural macro.

```
lazy_static! {
    static ref USERNAME: Regex = Regex::new("^[a-z0-9_-]{3,16}$").unwrap();
}
```
The implementation shows how to trigger custom warnings and error messages on the macro input.

```
warning: come on, pick a more creative name
  --> src/main.rs:10:16
   |
10 |     static ref FOO: String = "lazy_static".to_owned();
   |                ^^^
```
[§](https://docs.rs#testing)Testing

When testing macros, we often care not just that the macro can be used
successfully but also that when the macro is provided with invalid input it
produces maximally helpful error messages. Consider using the [ trybuild](https://github.com/dtolnay/trybuild)
crate to write tests for errors that are emitted by your macro or errors
detected by the Rust compiler in the expanded code following misuse of the
macro. Such tests help avoid regressions from later refactors that
mistakenly make an error no longer trigger or be less helpful than it used
to be.

[§](https://docs.rs#debugging)Debugging

When developing a procedural macro it can be helpful to look at what the
generated code looks like. Use `cargo rustc -- -Zunstable-options -Zunpretty=expanded` or the [ cargo expand](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-expand) subcommand.

To show the expanded code for some crate that uses your procedural macro,
run `cargo expand` from that crate. To show the expanded code for one of
your own test cases, run `cargo expand --test the_test_case` where the last
argument is the name of the test file without the `.rs` extension.

This write-up by Brandon W Maister discusses debugging in more detail:
[Debugging Rust’s new Custom Derive system](https://quodlibetor.github.io/posts/debugging-rusts-new-custom-derive-system/).

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

Syn puts a lot of functionality behind optional features in order to optimize compile time for the most common use cases. The following features are available.

- `derive`- *(enabled by default)*— Data structures for representing the possible input to a derive macro, including structs and enums and types.
- `full`
- `parsing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to parse input tokens into a syntax tree node of a chosen type.
- `printing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to print a syntax tree node as tokens of Rust source code.
- `visit`
- `visit-mut`
- `fold`
- `clone-impls`- *(enabled by default)*— Clone impls for all syntax tree types.
- `extra-traits`
- `proc-macro`- *(enabled by default)*— Runtime dependency on the dynamic library libproc_macro from rustc toolchain.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [buffer](https://docs.rs/buffer/index.html)- `parsing`
- A stably addressed token buffer supporting efficient traversal based on a cheaply copyable cursor.
- [ext](https://docs.rs/ext/index.html)
- Extension traits to provide parsing methods on foreign types.
- [fold](https://docs.rs/fold/index.html)- `fold`
- Syntax tree traversal to transform the nodes of an owned syntax tree.
- [meta](https://docs.rs/meta/index.html)- `parsing`and (- `derive`or- `full`)
- Facility for interpreting structured content inside of an `Attribute`.
- [parse](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)- `parsing`
- Parsing interface for parsing a token stream into a syntax tree node.
- [punctuated](https://docs.rs/punctuated/index.html)
- A punctuated sequence of syntax tree nodes separated by punctuation.
- [spanned](https://docs.rs/spanned/index.html)- `parsing`and- `printing`
- A trait that can provide the `Span`of the complete contents of a syntax tree node.
- [token](https://docs.rs/token/index.html)
- Tokens representing Rust punctuation, keywords, and delimiters.
- [visit](https://docs.rs/visit/index.html)- `visit`
- Syntax tree traversal to walk a shared borrow of a syntax tree.
- [visit_](https://docs.rs/visit_mut/index.html)- mut - `visit-mut`
- Syntax tree traversal to mutate an exclusive borrow of a syntax tree in place.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [Token](https://docs.rs/macro.Token.html)
- A type-macro that expands to the name of the Rust type representation of a given token.
- [braced](https://docs.rs/macro.braced.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of curly braces and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [bracketed](https://docs.rs/macro.bracketed.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of square brackets and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_keyword.html)- keyword
- Define a type that supports parsing and printing a given identifier as if it were a keyword.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_punctuation.html)- punctuation
- Define a type that supports parsing and printing a multi-character symbol as if it were a punctuation token.
- [parenthesized](https://docs.rs/macro.parenthesized.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of parentheses and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_macro_input.html)- macro_ - input - `parsing`and- `proc-macro`
- Parse the input TokenStream of a macro, triggering a compile error if the tokens fail to parse.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_quote.html)- quote - `parsing`and- `printing`
- Quasi-quotation macro that accepts input like the `quote!`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_quote_spanned.html)- quote_ - spanned - `parsing`and- `printing`
- This macro is `parse_quote!``quote_spanned!`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Abi](https://docs.rs/struct.Abi.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- The binary interface of a function: `extern "C"`.
- [Angle](https://docs.rs/struct.AngleBracketedGenericArguments.html)- Bracketed - Generic - Arguments - `derive`or- `full`
- Angle bracketed arguments of a path segment: the `<K, V>`in`HashMap<K, V>`.
- [Arm](https://docs.rs/struct.Arm.html)- `full`
- One arm of a `match`expression:`0..=10 => { return true; }`.
- [Assoc](https://docs.rs/struct.AssocConst.html)- Const - `derive`or- `full`
- An equality constraint on an associated constant: the `PANIC = false`in`Trait<PANIC = false>`.
- [Assoc](https://docs.rs/struct.AssocType.html)- Type - `derive`or- `full`
- A binding (equality constraint) on an associated type: the `Item = u8`in`Iterator<Item = u8>`.
- [Attribute](https://docs.rs/struct.Attribute.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- An attribute, like `#[repr(transparent)]`.
- [Bare](https://docs.rs/struct.BareFnArg.html)- FnArg - `derive`or- `full`
- An argument in a function type: the `usize`in`fn(usize) -> bool`.
- [Bare](https://docs.rs/struct.BareVariadic.html)- Variadic - `derive`or- `full`
- The variadic argument of a function pointer like `fn(usize, ...)`.
- [Block](https://docs.rs/struct.Block.html)- `full`
- A braced block containing Rust statements.
- [Bound](https://docs.rs/struct.BoundLifetimes.html)- Lifetimes - `derive`or- `full`
- A set of bound lifetimes: `for<'a, 'b, 'c>`.
- [Const](https://docs.rs/struct.ConstParam.html)- Param - `derive`or- `full`
- A const generic parameter: `const LENGTH: usize`.
- [Constraint](https://docs.rs/struct.Constraint.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- An associated type bound: `Iterator<Item: Display>`.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/struct.DataEnum.html)- Enum - `derive`
- An enum input to a `proc_macro_derive`macro.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/struct.DataStruct.html)- Struct - `derive`
- A struct input to a `proc_macro_derive`macro.
- [Data](https://docs.rs/struct.DataUnion.html)- Union - `derive`
- An untagged union input to a `proc_macro_derive`macro.
- [Derive](https://docs.rs/struct.DeriveInput.html)- Input - `derive`
- Data structure sent to a `proc_macro_derive`macro.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- Error returned when a Syn parser cannot parse the input tokens.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprArray.html)- Array - `full`
- A slice literal expression: `[a, b, c, d]`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprAssign.html)- Assign - `full`
- An assignment expression: `a = compute()`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprAsync.html)- Async - `full`
- An async block: `async { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprAwait.html)- Await - `full`
- An await expression: `fut.await`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprBinary.html)- Binary - `derive`or- `full`
- A binary operation: `a + b`,`a += b`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprBlock.html)- Block - `full`
- A blocked scope: `{ ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprBreak.html)- Break - `full`
- A `break`, with an optional label to break and an optional expression.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprCall.html)- Call - `derive`or- `full`
- A function call expression: `invoke(a, b)`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprCast.html)- Cast - `derive`or- `full`
- A cast expression: `foo as f64`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprClosure.html)- Closure - `full`
- A closure expression: `|a, b| a + b`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprConst.html)- Const - `full`
- A const block: `const { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprContinue.html)- Continue - `full`
- A `continue`, with an optional label.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprField.html)- Field - `derive`or- `full`
- Access of a named struct field (`obj.k`) or unnamed tuple struct field (`obj.0`).
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprForLoop.html)- ForLoop - `full`
- A for loop: `for pat in expr { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprGroup.html)- Group - `full`
- An expression contained within invisible delimiters.
- [ExprIf](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprIf.html)- `full`
- An `if`expression with an optional`else`block:`if expr { ... } else { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprIndex.html)- Index - `derive`or- `full`
- A square bracketed indexing expression: `vector[2]`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprInfer.html)- Infer - `full`
- The inferred value of a const generic argument, denoted `_`.
- [ExprLet](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprLet.html)- `full`
- A `let`guard:`let Some(x) = opt`.
- [ExprLit](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprLit.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A literal in place of an expression: `1`,`"foo"`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprLoop.html)- Loop - `full`
- Conditionless loop: `loop { ... }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprMacro.html)- Macro - `derive`or- `full`
- A macro invocation expression: `format!("{}", q)`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprMatch.html)- Match - `full`
- A `match`expression:`match n { Some(n) => {}, None => {} }`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprMethodCall.html)- Method - Call - `derive`or- `full`
- A method call expression: `x.foo::<T>(a, b)`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprParen.html)- Paren - `derive`or- `full`
- A parenthesized expression: `(a + b)`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprPath.html)- Path - `derive`or- `full`
- A path like `core::mem::replace`possibly containing generic parameters and a qualified self-type.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprRange.html)- Range - `full`

- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprRawAddr.html)- RawAddr - `full`

- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprReference.html)- Reference - `derive`or- `full`
- A referencing operation: `&a`or`&mut a`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprRepeat.html)- Repeat - `full`
- An array literal constructed from one repeated element: `[0u8; N]`.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprReturn.html)- Return - `full`
- A `return`, with an optional value to be returned.
- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprStruct.html)- Struct - `derive`or- `full`

- [ExprTry](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprTry.html)- `full`

- [Expr](https://docs.rs/struct.ExprTuple.html)- Tuple - `full`

- [Fields](https://docs.rs/struct.FieldsUnnamed.html)- Unnamed - `derive`or- `full`

- [File](https://docs.rs/struct.File.html)- `full`

- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemEnum.html)- Enum - `full`

- [ItemFn](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemFn.html)- `full`

- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemForeignMod.html)- Foreign - Mod - `full`

- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemImpl.html)- Impl - `full`

- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemMacro.html)- Macro - `full`

- [Item](https://docs.rs/struct.ItemStruct.html)- Struct - `full`

- A Rust lifetime: `'a`.

- [Local](https://docs.rs/struct.Local.html)- `full`

- [Macro](https://docs.rs/struct.Macro.html)- `derive`or- `full`

- [Meta](https://docs.rs/struct.MetaList.html)- List - `derive`or- `full`

- [PatOr](https://docs.rs/struct.PatOr.html)- `full`

- [Predicate](https://docs.rs/struct.PredicateType.html)- Type - `derive`or- `full`

- [QSelf](https://docs.rs/struct.QSelf.html)- `derive`or- `full`

- [Receiver](https://docs.rs/struct.Receiver.html)- `full`
- The `self`argument of an associated method.
- [Signature](https://docs.rs/struct.Signature.html)- `full`
- A function signature in a trait or implementation: `unsafe fn initialize(&self)`.
- [Stmt](https://docs.rs/struct.StmtMacro.html)- Macro - `full`
- A macro invocation in statement position.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/struct.TraitBound.html)- Bound - `derive`or- `full`
- A trait used as a bound on a type parameter.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/struct.TraitItemConst.html)- Item - Const - `full`
- An associated constant within the definition of a trait.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/struct.TraitItemFn.html)- Item - Fn - `full`
- An associated function within the definition of a trait.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/struct.TraitItemMacro.html)- Item - Macro - `full`
- A macro invocation within the definition of a trait.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/struct.TraitItemType.html)- Item - Type - `full`
- An associated type within the definition of a trait.

# solana_address - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-address/^2.6.1/

## Expand description

Address representation for Solana.

An address is a sequence of 32 bytes, often shown as a base58 encoded string (e.g. 14grJpemFaf88c8tiVb77W7TYg2W3ir6pfkKz3YjhhZ5).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [address](https://docs.rs/macro.address.html)- `decode`
- Convenience macro to define a static `Address`value.
- [declare_](https://docs.rs/macro.declare_deprecated_id.html)- deprecated_ - id - `decode`
- Same as `declare_id`
- [declare_](https://docs.rs/macro.declare_id.html)- id - `decode`
- Convenience macro to declare a static address and functions to interact with it.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Address](https://docs.rs/struct.Address.html)
- The address of a [Solana account](https://solana.com/docs/core/accounts).
- [Address](https://docs.rs/struct.AddressHasher.html)- Hasher - `rand`and neither- `target_os=solana`nor BPF
- A faster, but less collision resistant hasher for addresses.
- [Address](https://docs.rs/struct.AddressHasherBuilder.html)- Hasher - Builder - `rand`and neither- `target_os=solana`nor BPF
- A builder for faster, but less collision resistant hasher for addresses.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [ADDRESS_](https://docs.rs/constant.ADDRESS_BYTES.html)- BYTES
- Number of bytes in an address.
- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_SEEDS.html)- SEEDS
- Maximum number of seeds
- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_SEED_LEN.html)- SEED_ - LEN
- maximum length of derived `Address`seed
- [PDA_](https://docs.rs/constant.PDA_MARKER.html)- MARKER - Non-BPF
- Marker used to find program derived addresses (PDAs).

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [address_](https://docs.rs/fn.address_eq.html)- eq
- Custom implementation of equality for `Address`.
- [bytes_](https://docs.rs/fn.bytes_are_curve_point.html)- are_ - curve_ - point - `curve25519`or- `syscalls`
- Check whether the given bytes represent a valid curve point.

---

# solana_address - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-address/^2.0.0/

## Expand description

Address representation for Solana.

An address is a sequence of 32 bytes, often shown as a base58 encoded string (e.g. 14grJpemFaf88c8tiVb77W7TYg2W3ir6pfkKz3YjhhZ5).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [address](https://docs.rs/macro.address.html)- `decode`
- Convenience macro to define a static `Address`value.
- [declare_](https://docs.rs/macro.declare_deprecated_id.html)- deprecated_ - id - `decode`
- Same as `declare_id`
- [declare_](https://docs.rs/macro.declare_id.html)- id - `decode`
- Convenience macro to declare a static address and functions to interact with it.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Address](https://docs.rs/struct.Address.html)
- The address of a [Solana account](https://solana.com/docs/core/accounts).
- [Address](https://docs.rs/struct.AddressHasher.html)- Hasher - `rand`and neither- `target_os=solana`nor BPF
- A faster, but less collision resistant hasher for addresses.
- [Address](https://docs.rs/struct.AddressHasherBuilder.html)- Hasher - Builder - `rand`and neither- `target_os=solana`nor BPF
- A builder for faster, but less collision resistant hasher for addresses.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [ADDRESS_](https://docs.rs/constant.ADDRESS_BYTES.html)- BYTES
- Number of bytes in an address.
- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_SEEDS.html)- SEEDS
- Maximum number of seeds
- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_SEED_LEN.html)- SEED_ - LEN
- maximum length of derived `Address`seed
- [PDA_](https://docs.rs/constant.PDA_MARKER.html)- MARKER - Non-BPF
- Marker used to find program derived addresses (PDAs).

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- Custom implementation of equality for `Address`.
- [bytes_](https://docs.rs/fn.bytes_are_curve_point.html)- are_ - curve_ - point - `curve25519`or- `syscalls`
- Check whether the given bytes represent a valid curve point.
